docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The laplace package consists of two main components:

  1. The subclasses of laplace.BaseLaplace that implement different sparsity structures: different subsets of weights ('all', 'subnetwork' and 'last_layer') and different structures of the Hessian approximation ('full', 'kron', 'lowrank', 'diag' and 'gp'). The weight-space and subset-of-data GP estimators include laplace.FullLaplace, laplace.KronLaplace, laplace.DiagLaplace, laplace.FunctionalLaplace, their last-layer variations, the subnetwork variants, and laplace.LowRankLaplace. The function-space ELLA and VaLLA variants are selected through the same laplace.Laplace function.
  2. The backends in laplace.curvature which provide access to Hessian approximations of the corresponding sparsity structures, for example, the diagonal GGN.

For hessian_structure="gp", the factory also accepts functional_approximation="sod" | "nystrom" | "variational". The latter two select ELLA and VaLLA, respectively. These and FunctionalLaplace share BaseFunctionalLaplace prediction and sampling methods, while each estimator implements its own fitting and posterior covariance. New function-space methods should implement _glm_predictive_distribution, fit, and method-specific checkpoint state; they must not inherit another method's marginal-likelihood formula by default.

The predictive-moment method returns a mean shaped [batch, outputs] and covariance shaped [batch, outputs, outputs]. With joint=True, flatten the mean to [batch * outputs] and return covariance shaped [batch * outputs, batch * outputs], ordered by input and then output. These moments exclude observation noise. Implement _refresh_posterior if changing hyperparameters invalidates cached posterior factors.

Reusable function-space helpers live in laplace/utils/functional_utils.py and are exported through laplace.utils. See the utilities API reference for sampling, batch handling, target shaping, and device conversion. Helpers prefixed with an underscore support specific estimator internals and are not part of the public API.

Additionally, the package provides utilities for decomposing a neural network into feature extractor and last layer for LLLaplace subclasses (laplace.utils.feature_extractor) and effectively dealing with Kronecker factors (laplace.utils.matrix).

Finally, the package implements several options to select/specify a subnetwork for SubnetLaplace (as subclasses of laplace.utils.subnetmask.SubnetMask). Automatic subnetwork selection strategies include: uniformly at random (laplace.utils.subnetmask.RandomSubnetMask), by largest parameter magnitudes (LargestMagnitudeSubnetMask), and by largest marginal parameter variances (LargestVarianceDiagLaplaceSubnetMask and LargestVarianceSWAGSubnetMask). In addition to that, subnetworks can also be specified manually, by listing the names of either the model parameters (ParamNameSubnetMask) or modules (ModuleNameSubnetMask) to perform Laplace inference over.

docs.title: Extendability
docs.text:
To extend the laplace package, new BaseLaplace subclasses can be designed, for example, Laplace with a block-diagonal Hessian structure. One can also implement custom subnetwork selection strategies as new subclasses of SubnetMask.

Alternatively, extending or integrating backends (subclasses of curvature.curvature) allows to provide different Hessian approximations to the Laplace approximations. For example, currently the curvature.CurvlinopsInterface based on Curvlinops and the native torch.func (previously known as functorch), curvature.BackPackInterface based on BackPACK and curvature.AsdlInterface based on ASDL are available.

docs.title: Example: Diffusion Models
docs.text:
In this example, we apply Laplace to a model whose output is an image, such as the denoiser of a diffusion model. The same recipe works for other image- or video-output models trained with a Gaussian likelihood. For per-pixel classification, see the semantic segmentation example.

Laplace expects the output axis to be the last one, e.g., (N, K) for standard models or (N, L, K) for language models. Convolutional models in PyTorch instead return (N, C, H, W), with the channels on axis 1. Laplace does not reorder the output for you, so you need to wrap your model so that it returns (N, H, W, C). The wrapper is a single movedim call. Your data loader must emit the targets in the same layout.

Intended usage

The wrapped model must return (N, H, W, C), and the targets must also be (N, H, W, C). Every pixel is an observation in the likelihood, i.e., the log-likelihood sums over all N * H * W pixels, each with a C-dimensional output.

First, the imports and some constants.

from collections.abc import MutableMapping

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset

from laplace import Laplace
from laplace.curvature import CurvlinopsGGN

torch.manual_seed(0)

N_DATA = 64
CHANNELS = 3  # C
HEIGHT = 8  # H
WIDTH = 8  # W

Next, we define a toy denoiser. It predicts the noise eps from a noisy image x_t and the diffusion time t, and returns its prediction in PyTorch's usual (N, C, H, W) layout. In practice, this would be the U-Net of your diffusion model.

class Denoiser(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.body = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(CHANNELS + 1, 16, 3, padding=1),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(16, 16, 3, padding=1),
            nn.SiLU(),
        )
        self.head = nn.Conv2d(16, CHANNELS, 1)

    def forward(self, x_t: torch.Tensor, t: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        t_map = t.view(-1, 1, 1, 1).expand(-1, 1, *x_t.shape[-2:])
        h = self.body(torch.cat([x_t, t_map], dim=1))
        return self.head(h)  # (N, C, H, W)

docs.title: Wrapping the model
docs.text:
The wrapper does two things. First, since the denoiser takes two inputs, it takes a single dict-like input and unpacks it, as in the Huggingface example. Second, it moves the channel axis of the output to the end. Notice that we also move the inputs to the right device inside forward.

class ChannelsLast(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, denoiser: nn.Module) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.denoiser = denoiser

    def forward(self, data: MutableMapping) -> torch.Tensor:
        device = next(self.parameters()).device
        x_t = data["x_t"].to(device)
        t = data["t"].to(device)
        return self.denoiser(x_t, t).movedim(1, -1)  # (N, H, W, C)

The dataset emits dicts as well. The target eps gets the same movedim so that it matches the wrapped model's output. Here we use random tensors in place of a real diffusion training set.

class NoisyImages(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, n_data: int) -> None:
        self.x_t = torch.randn(n_data, CHANNELS, HEIGHT, WIDTH)
        self.t = torch.rand(n_data)
        self.eps = torch.randn(n_data, CHANNELS, HEIGHT, WIDTH)

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.t)

    def __getitem__(self, i: int) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
        return {
            "x_t": self.x_t[i],
            "t": self.t[i],
            "eps": self.eps[i].movedim(0, -1),  # (H, W, C)
        }


dataloader = DataLoader(NoisyImages(N_DATA), batch_size=16)
data = next(iter(dataloader))

model = ChannelsLast(Denoiser())
# Train it as usual
model.eval()

out = model.denoiser(data["x_t"], data["t"])
print(f"Output of the original model: {tuple(out.shape)}")
print(f"Output of the wrapped model: {tuple(model(data).shape)}")

Output of the original model: (16, 3, 8, 8)
Output of the wrapped model: (16, 8, 8, 3)

docs.title: Reproducing BayesDiff and FLARE
docs.text: Image outputs are large. A single example has H * W * C outputs, so the Jacobian that the GLM predictive needs has H * W * C rows per example and one column per parameter in the Laplace approximation. For a 64x64 RGB image, that is 12,288 rows. Diffusion papers keep this affordable by putting the Laplace approximation on a small part of the denoiser. BayesDiff uses the last layer, while FLARE uses a random subset of the weights. Below we set up both on the toy denoiser. They use the Curvlinops backend; see the caveats at the end for why.

docs.title: BayesDiff: diagonal last-layer Laplace
docs.text:
BayesDiff fits a last-layer Laplace approximation with a diagonal Hessian and estimates the variance of eps by sampling weights from the posterior, with 100 samples.

Laplace's own last-layer option (subset_of_weights="last_layer") only supports nn.Linear last layers, and the head here is a convolution. To get the same effect, switch off the gradients of every other layer and set subset_of_weights="all". Laplace only computes the Hessian and the Jacobians of parameters with requires_grad=True. The same trick works for any set of layers.

The sampling predictive (pred_type="nn") needs link_approx="mc". It runs the model once per weight sample and never computes the Jacobian.

for p in model.denoiser.body.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False

la = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="diag",
    backend=CurvlinopsGGN,
    dict_key_x="x_t",
    dict_key_y="eps",
)
la.fit(dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

f_mu, f_var = la(data, pred_type="nn", link_approx="mc", n_samples=100)
print(f"[BayesDiff] Mean: {tuple(f_mu.shape)}, variance: {tuple(f_var.shape)}")

[BayesDiff] Mean: (16, 8, 8, 3), variance: (16, 8, 8, 3)

The variance has one entry per pixel and channel, in the wrapped layout. To get back to (N, C, H, W), e.g., to plot a per-pixel uncertainty map, undo the movedim:

f_var = f_var.movedim(-1, 1)
print(f"[BayesDiff] Variance in (N, C, H, W): {tuple(f_var.shape)}")

[BayesDiff] Variance in (N, C, H, W): (16, 3, 8, 8)

docs.title: FLARE: full Laplace over a random subnetwork
docs.text:
FLARE argues that a last-layer Laplace approximation is not enough for diffusion models. It draws a uniformly random subset of the weights once, fits a full GGN over that subset, and pushes the posterior through the linearized denoiser, i.e., \(J \Sigma J^\top\), where \(J\) is the Jacobian of the denoiser with respect to the subset and \(\Sigma\) is the posterior covariance.

This maps to subnetwork Laplace (subset_of_weights="subnetwork") with the GLM predictive. Subnetwork Laplace takes the indices of the chosen weights in the flattened parameter vector, i.e., torch.nn.utils.parameters_to_vector(model.parameters()). RandomSubnetMask picks them uniformly at random. Other masks in laplace.utils, such as LargestMagnitudeSubnetMask, pick them by a score instead. With a few hundred weights, a full Hessian is cheap.

from laplace.utils import RandomSubnetMask

model = ChannelsLast(Denoiser())
model.eval()

subnetwork_mask = RandomSubnetMask(model, n_params_subnet=500)
subnetwork_indices = subnetwork_mask.select()

la = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    subset_of_weights="subnetwork",
    hessian_structure="full",
    subnetwork_indices=subnetwork_indices,
    backend=CurvlinopsGGN,
    dict_key_x="x_t",
    dict_key_y="eps",
)
la.fit(dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

f_mu, f_var = la(data, pred_type="glm", diagonal_output=True)
print(f"[FLARE] Hessian: {tuple(la.H.shape)}")
print(f"[FLARE] Mean: {tuple(f_mu.shape)}, variance: {tuple(f_var.shape)}")

[FLARE] Hessian: (500, 500)
[FLARE] Mean: (16, 8, 8, 3), variance: (16, 8, 8, 3)

With diagonal_output=True, you get the diagonal of \(J \Sigma J^\top\), the same shape as the mean. Without it, you get a C x C covariance per pixel, i.e., a tensor of shape (N, H, W, C, C).

FLARE scores each generated sample by the trace of its epistemic covariance divided by the output dimension. Only the diagonal is needed for that:

score = f_var.flatten(start_dim=1).mean(dim=1)
print(f"[FLARE] Score: {tuple(score.shape)}")

[FLARE] Score: (16,)

FLARE also carries this covariance through the reverse diffusion steps and takes the score at the final step. That recursion sits outside Laplace; the snippet above gives you the per-step term.

docs.title: Other options
docs.text: A diagonal Hessian over all weights also works with the GLM predictive, and so does K-FAC (hessian_structure="kron"), which is cheap to fit for large models. When the Jacobians of the GLM predictive do not fit in memory, use the sampling predictive (pred_type="nn" with link_approx="mc"), as in BayesDiff. It works with any Hessian structure.

docs.title: Video outputs
docs.text: The recipe is the same for video. A model with output (N, C, T, H, W) is wrapped with .movedim(1, -1) so that it returns (N, T, H, W, C), and the targets get the same layout. Diagonal and full Hessians work as above. K-FAC currently does not support nn.Conv3d layers.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Use the Curvlinops backends (CurvlinopsGGN, CurvlinopsEF). The ASDL and BackPACK backends raise an error for image outputs.
  • subset_of_weights="last_layer" requires an nn.Linear last layer. Use the requires_grad approach from the BayesDiff section for convolutional heads.

The full script is in examples/diffusion_example.py.

docs.title: Example: ELLA and VaLLA
docs.text:
Exact linearized Laplace needs the full GGN of the network. That is fine for a small MLP, but it does not scale. ELLA and VaLLA both approximate the same linearized-Laplace GP in function space, so they work with larger networks but using subsampled data. ELLA builds a low-rank Nyström basis from parameter Jacobians. VaLLA fits a sparse variational GP with inducing points.

In this example we fit both to the sinusoidal regression task from the regression example and compare them with exact LA. Both methods leave the network weights alone. You train a MAP network as usual and fit the posterior afterwards.

import torch

from laplace import Laplace

from helper.dataloaders import get_sinusoid_example

torch.manual_seed(711)
X_train, y_train, train_loader, X_test = get_sinusoid_example(sigma_noise=0.3)

docs.title: Training a MAP
docs.text:
Nothing new here. We train a single-hidden-layer Tanh network, reseeding first so the initialization doesn't depend on the data sampling above:

torch.manual_seed(711)
model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(1, 50), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(50, 1)
)

criterion = torch.nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for i in range(1000):
    for X, y in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(X), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

docs.title: Exact linearized Laplace
docs.text:
As a reference, we fit a full-GGN Laplace approximation. The network has only 151 parameters, so this is cheap.

We generated the data with noise \(\sigma = 0.3\), so we pass that value as sigma_noise and only tune the prior precision. This assumes the aleatoric noise is known. If it isn't, optimize the noise together with the prior precision through the marginal likelihood, as in the regression example.

la = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="full",
    sigma_noise=0.3,
)
la.fit(train_loader)
la.optimize_prior_precision(method="marglik")

docs.title: ELLA
docs.text:
ELLA (Deng, Zhou, and Zhu) is selected with hessian_structure="gp" and functional_approximation="nystrom". During fit, it draws subsample_size training inputs, computes the network's parameter Jacobians on them, and keeps the top n_eigenvalues directions of the resulting kernel as a Nyström basis. It then accumulates the GGN in that basis over the full loader. Think of subsample_size as how much of the data gets a say in the basis, and n_eigenvalues as how many directions you keep. n_eigenvalues must be positive and at most subsample_size, which in turn can't exceed the number of training rows.

We have 150 points, so 100 of them for the basis and a rank of 20 is plenty:

ella = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="gp",
    functional_approximation="nystrom",
    subsample_size=100,
    n_eigenvalues=20,
    sigma_noise=la.sigma_noise.item(),
    prior_precision=la.prior_precision.item(),
)
ella.fit(train_loader)

If you ask for more directions than the sampled kernel actually has, fit raises a ValueError that tells you the usable rank. That happens when the subsample is too small or too redundant. Lower n_eigenvalues, raise subsample_size, or try another seed.

The basis selection and the GGN accumulation each draw from the loader separately. With a shuffling loader they may see different rows. ella.n_data records how many examples went into the GGN.

We reuse the noise and prior precision from the exact LA, so ELLA's predictive is directly comparable to it. The prior has to be a positive scalar precision with zero mean. ELLA has no GP marginal likelihood, so to tune the prior precision on its own you need held-out data:

ella.optimize_prior_precision(method="gridsearch", val_loader=val_loader)

Passing validation data also makes ella.fit_history_ record the validation negative log likelihood next to the processed example counts.

docs.title: VaLLA
docs.text:
VaLLA (Ortega, Rodríguez Santana, and Hernández-Lobato) takes a different route to the same GP. Instead of a fixed basis, it places num_inducing inducing points in input space and fits a variational posterior over the function values there. It is selected with functional_approximation="variational".

The inducing points need a starting position. inducing_locations="random" picks them from the training inputs, and "kmeans" places them at k-means centroids, which only works for floating-point tensor inputs. You can also pass a tensor of locations yourself. Floating-point locations then move during fitting. Integer tensors and mapping-style inputs stay where you put them, and only the variational factor and hyperparameters are optimized.

alpha picks the divergence that VaLLA minimizes. The default alpha=1.0 is the alpha-divergence objective from the paper, and alpha=0.0 gives the usual ELBO. Here we place 30 inducing points with k-means and fit the ELBO:

valla = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="gp",
    functional_approximation="variational",
    inducing_locations="kmeans",
    num_inducing=30,
    alpha=0.0,
    sigma_noise=la.sigma_noise.item(),
    prior_precision=la.prior_precision.item(),
)
valla.fit(train_loader, iterations=3000, lr=1e-3)

Unlike ELLA, fit runs an optimizer over minibatches for iterations steps at learning rate lr, with the network weights held fixed. It updates the variational factor and the inducing locations. The prior precision and observation noise from the exact LA are only starting values here, and the optimizer tunes them too, which is why VaLLA doesn't need a separate optimize_prior_precision call.

The objective at each step is in valla.fit_history_["objective"]. If the curve hasn't flattened, keep going from where you stopped (the figure below doesn't do this):

valla.fit(train_loader, iterations=500, lr=1e-3, override=False)

Without override=False, a second fit starts the inducing points and variational factor over, but keeps the learned prior precision and noise.

docs.title: Predictive
docs.text:
All three objects are called the same way. For regression they return the MAP mean and the latent variance. Add the observation noise to get the predictive variance of \(y\). For VaLLA, that is the noise it learned during fitting. The figure shows the mean with a band of two predictive standard deviations:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = X_test.flatten()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, sharey=True, figsize=(11, 2.8))

def panel(ax, title, f_mu, f_var=None, sigma_noise=None):
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.scatter(X_train.flatten(), y_train.flatten(), alpha=0.3, color="tab:orange", s=8)
    f_mu = f_mu.detach().flatten()
    ax.plot(x, f_mu, color="black", lw=1)
    if f_var is not None:
        std = (f_var.detach().flatten() + sigma_noise**2).sqrt()
        ax.fill_between(x, f_mu - 2 * std, f_mu + 2 * std, alpha=0.3, color="tab:blue")
    ax.set_xlim(x.min(), x.max())
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")

with torch.no_grad():
    panel(axes[0], "MAP", model(X_test))

for ax, (name, posterior) in zip(
    axes[1:], [("Exact LA", la), ("ELLA", ella), ("VaLLA", valla)]
):
    panel(ax, name, *posterior(X_test), sigma_noise=posterior.sigma_noise.item())

axes[0].set_ylim([-4, 6])
axes[0].set_ylabel("$y$")
plt.tight_layout()

ELLA is very close to exact LA here. For a 1D problem and 151 parameters, a rank-20 basis is apparently enough. Inside the data region, all three bands stay close to the observation noise. Away from the data, VaLLA's bands are wider than exact LA on the left and narrower on the right. It learned its own prior precision and noise and works through 30 inducing points, so some difference from exact LA is expected.

ELLA fits in a single pass with no optimizer, but you have to choose subsample_size and n_eigenvalues yourself. VaLLA is more expensive to fit and adds an optimization loop, and it learns its hyperparameters as it goes.

docs.title: Beyond regression
docs.text:
Both methods also handle classification and reward modeling, and the call pattern stays the same. For classification, posterior(x) returns class probabilities. For reward modeling, it returns a (mean, covariance) tuple for the rewards of individual inputs, shaped [batch, 1] and [batch, 1, 1], so unpack it as you would in regression. VaLLA has two classification-specific knobs. When you pass inducing locations yourself, inducing_classes says which output each one belongs to (class 0 by default). mc_softmax_samples switches the data term from the default probit approximation to Monte Carlo sampling, and you need it for any alpha other than 1.

If you need joint predictions across inputs, for instance for Bayesian optimization, pass joint=True to predictive_moments, functional_samples, or predictive_samples. The samples come back shaped [samples, batch, outputs]. Neither method has weight-space sample, since the posterior lives in function space.

To save a fitted posterior, use state_dict and load_state_dict. For ELLA this stores the Nyström basis, and for VaLLA the inducing and variational state. The checkpoint holds the posterior only, not the network. Load it into a posterior built around the same pretrained model, with the same input keys, curvature backend, backend options, and backpropagation setting. load_state_dict checks that the model's weights and buffers match the checkpoint. It also restores the seed, and for VaLLA the random-generator state used in Monte Carlo fitting.

The full option list is in the ELLA and VaLLA API reference. python -m examples.ella and python -m examples.valla are minimal scripts that fit each method and print the output shapes.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Often, we want to compute non-analytic expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{p(f(x) \mid \mathcal{D})} [g(f(x))]\) of a function \(g(f(x))\) given a Laplace posterior over functions \(p(f(x) \mid \mathcal{D})\) at input \(x\). This naturally arises in decision-making: Given a posterior belief about an unknown function \(f\), we would like to compute the expected utility of \(x\). In Bayesian optimization, this is called _acquisition function_. For some utility function \(g\) and posterior belief \(p(f(x) \mid \mathcal{D})\), the resulting acquisition function can be computed analytically, e.g. if \(g\) is linear and the posterior is Gaussian (process). But, in general, closed-form solutions don't exist.

In this example, we will see how easy it is to compute a differentiable, Monte-Carlo approximated acquisition function under the posterior distribution over neural network functions implied by a Laplace approximation.

docs.title: Laplace approximations
docs.text:
As always, the first step of a Laplace approximation is MAP estimation.

import torch
import torch.utils.data as data_utils
from torch import autograd, nn, optim

from laplace import Laplace
from laplace.utils.enums import HessianStructure, Likelihood, PredType, SubsetOfWeights

torch.manual_seed(123)

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 10), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(10, 1))
X, Y = torch.randn(5, 2), torch.randn(5, 1)
train_loader = data_utils.DataLoader(data_utils.TensorDataset(X, Y), batch_size=3)
opt = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=5e-4)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

for epoch in range(10):
    model.train()

    for x, y in train_loader:
        opt.zero_grad()
        out = model(x)
        loss = loss_fn(out, y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

Then, we are ready to obtain the Laplace approximation. In this example, we focus on the weight-space approximation, but the same can be done in the function space directly by simply specifying hessian_structure=HessianStructure.GP.

la = Laplace(
    model,
    Likelihood.REGRESSION,
    subset_of_weights=SubsetOfWeights.ALL,
    hessian_structure=HessianStructure.KRON,
    enable_backprop=True,
)
la.fit(train_loader)
la.optimize_prior_precision(PredType.GLM)

Tip

If you need the gradient of quantities that depend on Laplace's predictive distribution/samples, then be sure to specify enable_backprop=True. This is in fact necessary for continuous Bayesian optimization.

docs.title: Thompson Sampling
docs.text:
The simplest acquisition function that can be obtained from the Laplace posterior is Thompson sampling. This is defined as \(a \sim p(f(x) \mid \mathcal{D})\). Thus, given la, it can be obtained very simply:

x_test = torch.randn(10, 2)
f_sample = la.functional_samples(x_test, n_samples=1)

Note that f_sample can be obtained through the "nn" and "glm" predictives. The la.functional_samples function supports both options.

for pred_type in [PredType.GLM, PredType.NN]:
    print(f"Thompson sampling, {pred_type}")

    x_test = torch.randn(10, 2)
    x_test.requires_grad = True

    f_sample = la.functional_samples(x_test, pred_type=pred_type, n_samples=1)
    f_sample = f_sample.squeeze(0)  # We only use a single sample
    print(f"TS shape: {f_sample.shape}, TS requires grad: {f_sample.requires_grad}")

    grad_x = autograd.grad(f_sample.sum(), x_test)[0]

    print(
        f"Grad x_test shape: {grad_x.shape}, Grad x_test vanishing: {torch.allclose(grad_x, torch.tensor(0.0))}"
    )
    print()

The snippet above will output:

Thompson sampling, glm
TS shape: torch.Size([10, 1]), TS requires grad: True
Grad x_test shape: torch.Size([10, 2]), Grad x_test vanishing: False

Thompson sampling, nn
TS shape: torch.Size([10, 1]), TS requires grad: True
Grad x_test shape: torch.Size([10, 2]), Grad x_test vanishing: False

As we can see, the gradient can be computed through Laplace's predictive and its non-vanishing.

docs.title: Monte-Carlo EI
docs.text:
In general, given a choice of utility function \(u(f(x))\), any acquisition function can be obtained w.r.t. the Laplace posterior. For example, to compute Monte-Carlo-approximated EI, we can do so via:

f_best = torch.tensor(0.123)  # Arbitrary in this example
f_samples = la.functional_samples(x_test, pred_type=pred_type, n_samples=10)
ei = (f_samples - f_best.reshape(1, 1, 1)).clamp(0.0).mean(0)

Again, if \(u\) is differentiable, then we can obtain the gradient w.r.t. the input, and we can do continuous Bayesian optimization.

docs.title: Example: Huggingface LLMs
docs.text:
In this example, we will see how to apply Laplace on a GPT2 Huggingface (HF) model. Laplace only has lightweight requirements for this; namely that the model's forward method must only take a single dict-like object (dict, UserDict, or in general, collections.abc.MutableMapping). This is entirely compatible with HF since HF's data loaders are assumed to emit an object derived from UserDict. However, you need to ensure this yourself --- you need to wrap the standard HF model to conform to that requirement. Also, you need to e.g. do torch.to(device) inside the said forward method.

Let's start with as usual with importing stuff.

from collections.abc import MutableMapping
from collections import UserDict
import numpy
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.utils.data as data_utils

from laplace import Laplace

import logging
import warnings

logging.basicConfig(level="ERROR")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

from transformers import ( # noqa: E402
    GPT2Config,
    GPT2ForSequenceClassification,
    GPT2Tokenizer,
    DataCollatorWithPadding,
    PreTrainedTokenizer,
)
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model # noqa: E402
from datasets import Dataset # noqa: E402

# make deterministic

torch.manual_seed(0)
numpy.random.seed(0)

Next, we create a toy dataset. You can use any HF datasets or your own, of course.

tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
tokenizer.pad_token_id = tokenizer.eos_token_id

data = [
    {"text": "Today is hot, but I will manage!!!!", "label": 1},
    {"text": "Tomorrow is cold", "label": 0},
    {"text": "Carpe diem", "label": 1},
    {"text": "Tempus fugit", "label": 1},
]
dataset = Dataset.from_list(data)

def tokenize(row):
    return tokenizer(row["text"])

dataset = dataset.map(tokenize, remove_columns=["text"])
dataset.set_format(type="torch", columns=["input_ids", "attention_mask", "label"])
dataloader = data_utils.DataLoader(
    dataset, batch_size=100, collate_fn=DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer)
)

data = next(iter(dataloader))
print(
    f"Huggingface data defaults to UserDict, which is a MutableMapping? {isinstance(data, UserDict)}"
)
for k, v in data.items():
    print(k, v.shape)

This is the output:

Huggingface data defaults to UserDict, which is a MutableMapping? True
input_ids torch.Size([4, 9])
attention_mask torch.Size([4, 9])
labels torch.Size([4])

docs.title: Laplace on a subset of an LLM's weights
docs.text:
Now, let's do the main "meat" of this example: Wrapping the HF model into a model that is compatible with Laplace. Notice that this wrapper just wraps the HF model and nothing else. Notice also we do inputs.to(device) inside self.forward().

class MyGPT2(nn.Module):
    """
    Huggingface LLM wrapper.

    Args:
        tokenizer: The tokenizer used for preprocessing the text data. Needed
            since the model needs to know the padding token id.
    """

    def __init__(self, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizer) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        config = GPT2Config.from_pretrained("gpt2")
        config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id
        config.num_labels = 2
        self.hf_model = GPT2ForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
            "gpt2", config=config
        )

    def forward(self, data: MutableMapping) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Custom forward function. Handles things like moving the
        input tensor to the correct device inside.

        Args:
            data: A dict-like data structure with `input_ids` inside.
                This is the default data structure assumed by Huggingface
                dataloaders.

        Returns:
            logits: An `(batch_size, n_classes)`-sized tensor of logits.
        """
        device = next(self.parameters()).device
        input_ids = data["input_ids"].to(device)
        attn_mask = data["attention_mask"].to(device)
        output_dict = self.hf_model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attn_mask)
        return output_dict.logits

model = MyGPT2(tokenizer)

Now, let's apply Laplace. Let's do a last-layer Laplace first. Notice that we add an argument feature_reduction there. This is because Huggingface models reduce the logits and not the features.

model = MyGPT2(tokenizer)
model.eval()

la = Laplace(
    model,
    likelihood="classification",
    subset_of_weights="last_layer",
    hessian_structure="full",
    # This must reflect faithfully the reduction technique used in the model
    # Otherwise, correctness is not guaranteed
    feature_reduction="pick_last",
)
la.fit(dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

X_test = next(iter(dataloader))
print(f"[Last-layer Laplace] The predictive tensor is of shape: {la(X_test).shape}.")

Here's the output:

[Last-layer Laplace] The predictive tensor is of shape: torch.Size([4, 2]).

docs.title: Subnetwork Laplace
docs.text:
Also, we can do the same thing by switching off the gradients of all layers except the top layer. Laplace will automatically only compute the Hessian (and Jacobians) of the parameters in which requires_grad is True.

Notice that you can "mix-and-match" this gradient switching. You can do a subnetwork Laplace easily by doing so!

model.eval()

# Enable grad only for the last layer

for p in model.hf_model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False

for p in model.hf_model.score.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = True

la = Laplace(
    model,
    # Will only hit the last-layer since it's the only one that is grad-enabled
    likelihood="classification",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="diag",
)
la.fit(dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

X_test = next(iter(dataloader))
print(f"[Subnetwork Laplace] The predictive tensor is of shape: {la(X_test).shape}.")

Here are the outputs to validate that Laplace works:

[Subnetwork Laplace] The predictive tensor is of shape: torch.Size([4, 2]).

docs.title: Full Laplace on LoRA parameters only
docs.text:
Of course, you can also apply Laplace on the parameter-efficient fine tuning weights (like LoRA). To do this, simply extend your LLM with LoRA, using HF's peft library, and apply Laplace as usual. Note that peft automatically switches off the non-LoRA weights.

def get_lora_model():
    model = MyGPT2(tokenizer) # Note we don't disable grad
    config = LoraConfig(
        r=4,
        lora_alpha=16,
        target_modules=["c_attn"], # LoRA on the attention weights
        lora_dropout=0.1,
        bias="none",
    )
    lora_model = get_peft_model(model, config)
    return lora_model

lora_model = get_lora_model()

# Train it as usual

lora_model.eval()

lora_la = Laplace(
    lora_model,
    likelihood="classification",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="kron",
)
lora_la.fit(dataloader)

X_test = next(iter(dataloader))
print(f"[LoRA-LLM] The predictive tensor is of shape: {lora_la(X_test).shape}.")

Here is the output, as expected:

[LoRA-LLM] The predictive tensor is of shape: torch.Size([4, 2]).

As a final note, the dict-like input requirement of Laplace is very flexible. It can essentially be applicable to any tasks and any models. You just need to wrap the said model and make sure that your data loaders emit dict-like objects, where the input tensors are the dicts' values.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
CurvlinopsEF with hessian_structure="diag", and subnetwork Laplace with CurvlinopsEF, compute per-example gradients with torch.func's vmap. vmap does not support data-dependent control flow, which Huggingface transformers use, e.g., when building the attention mask. So these combinations raise an error for Huggingface models, whether the model's forward takes a dict or a single tensor.

Instead, choose one of the following backends:

  • CurvlinopsGGN for hessian_factorization = {"kron", "diag"}
  • CurvlinopsEF for hessian_factorization = {"kron"}
  • AsdlGGN for hessian_factorization = {"kron", "diag"}
  • AsdlEF for hessian_factorization = {"kron", "diag"}

docs.title: Example: Language Modeling
docs.text:
In this example, we apply Laplace to sequence models, where the inputs have 3 axes (batch size, sequence length, and input dimensionality) and so do the outputs (batch size, sequence length, and output dimensionality). We start with a model that outputs a vector per token, trained with a Gaussian likelihood. Then we turn to next-token prediction, i.e., language modeling, which is classification with one set of logits per token.

Let's start with defining a toy model. Notice that laplace-torch requires the model to take a single input, which can be a dictionary. See the following explanation.

Intended usage

The model is assumed to take batch-first inputs with one output per token, i.e., inputs are (B, L, D) and outputs are (B, L, K). Each of the B * L tokens is an observation in the likelihood. The ASDL backends (AsdlEF, AsdlGGN) rely on this layout. For other layouts, e.g., outputs pooled over tokens (B, K) or sequence-first layers (L, B, D), use the Curvlinops backends (CurvlinopsEF, CurvlinopsGGN) instead.

# `tensordict` is only needed for this toy dataset: `pip install tensordict`
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from tensordict import TensorDict
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from laplace import Laplace
from laplace.curvature.asdl import AsdlEF, AsdlGGN
from laplace.utils.enums import LinkApprox, PredType

BATCH_SIZE = 4  # B
SEQ_LENGTH = 6  # L
EMBED_DIM = 8  # D
OUTPUT_SIZE = 2  # K
INPUT_KEY = "input"
OUTPUT_KEY = "output"


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        # Batch first to follow the intended usage, otherwise MultiheadAttention will take `(L, B, D)`
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(EMBED_DIM, num_heads=1, batch_first=True)
        self.final_layer = nn.Linear(EMBED_DIM, OUTPUT_SIZE)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x[INPUT_KEY].view(-1, SEQ_LENGTH, EMBED_DIM)  # (B, L, D)
        out = self.attn(x, x, x, need_weights=False)[0]  # (B, L, D)
        return self.final_layer(out)  # (B, L, K)

Next, we create a toy dataset. You can use any HF datasets or your own, of course.

ds = TensorDict(
    {
        INPUT_KEY: torch.randn((100, SEQ_LENGTH, EMBED_DIM)),
        OUTPUT_KEY: torch.randn((100, SEQ_LENGTH, OUTPUT_SIZE)),
    },
    batch_size=[100],
)  # simulates a dataset
dl = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, collate_fn=lambda x: x)

model = Model()

Suppose we want to do a last-layer Laplace approximation. Then the easiest way to do this is by switching off the gradients of all but the final layer. Of course we can also do a subnetwork/full Laplace by mix-and-match the gradient requirements.

model = Model()

for mod_name, mod in model.named_modules():
    if mod_name == "final_layer":
        for p in mod.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = True
    else:
        for p in mod.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False

# GLM
la = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    hessian_structure="full",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    backend=AsdlEF,
    dict_key_x=INPUT_KEY,
    dict_key_y=OUTPUT_KEY,
    enable_backprop=False,  # True => functorch Jacobian, False => ASDL Jacobian
)
la.fit(dl)

Note

When enable_backprop = True, the Jacobian in the GLM predictive is obtained through functorch (torch.func). There is currently some memory inefficiency with this approach. Also, currently, only the ASDL and Curvlinops backends are supported.

Let's inspect the predictive distributions of this model. For MAP estimate, this yields a (B, L, K) tensor.

data = next(iter(dl))
pred_map = model(data)

For the GLM predictive of Laplace:

pred_la_mean, pred_la_var = la(data, pred_type=PredType.GLM)
print(pred_la_mean.shape, pred_la_var.shape)

pred_la_mean, pred_la_var = la(data, pred_type=PredType.GLM, diagonal_output=True)
print(pred_la_mean.shape, pred_la_var.shape)

we will get shapes (B, L, K) for the mean tensor and (B, L, K, K) for the variance tensor by default. When diagonal_output=True, the variance tensor will instead be (B, L, K) as expected.

For the NN/sampled predictive:

# MC
la = Laplace(
    model,
    "regression",
    hessian_structure="diag",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    backend=AsdlGGN,
    dict_key_x=INPUT_KEY,
    dict_key_y=OUTPUT_KEY,
)
la.fit(dl)

pred_la_mean, pred_la_var = la(
    data, pred_type=PredType.NN, link_approx=LinkApprox.MC, n_samples=10
)
print(pred_la_mean.shape, pred_la_var.shape)

we get two (B, L, K) tensors.

docs.title: Next-token prediction
docs.text:
For language modeling, the model returns logits of shape (B, L, V), where V is the vocabulary size, and the targets are the token ids of shape (B, L). This is classification, and, as before, each of the B * L tokens is an observation in the likelihood. The class axis must be the last one, as is usual for language models, and the targets must be class indices. Class probabilities as targets are only supported for logits of shape (B, C).

Below is a toy causal language model. It takes the token ids under "input_ids" and predicts the next token at every position.

from laplace.curvature.curvlinops import CurvlinopsGGN

VOCAB_SIZE = 20  # V
IDS_KEY = "input_ids"
LABELS_KEY = "labels"


class CausalLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(VOCAB_SIZE, EMBED_DIM)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(EMBED_DIM, num_heads=1, batch_first=True)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(EMBED_DIM, VOCAB_SIZE)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.embedding(x[IDS_KEY])  # (B, L, D)
        L = x.shape[1]
        causal_mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(L, L, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
        out = self.attn(x, x, x, attn_mask=causal_mask, need_weights=False)[0]
        return self.lm_head(out)  # (B, L, V)

The label of each token is the token that follows it:

tokens = torch.randint(VOCAB_SIZE, (100, SEQ_LENGTH + 1))
ds = TensorDict(
    {IDS_KEY: tokens[:, :-1], LABELS_KEY: tokens[:, 1:]},
    batch_size=[100],
)
dl = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, collate_fn=lambda x: x)

The LM head of a real model has V * D weights, so we use a Kronecker-factored Hessian over the head only:

model = CausalLM()

for mod_name, mod in model.named_modules():
    for p in mod.parameters(recurse=False):
        p.requires_grad = mod_name == "lm_head"

la = Laplace(
    model,
    "classification",
    hessian_structure="kron",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    backend=CurvlinopsGGN,
    dict_key_x=IDS_KEY,
    dict_key_y=LABELS_KEY,
)
la.fit(dl)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

Both predictives return the next-token probabilities at every position, i.e., a (B, L, V) tensor:

data = next(iter(dl))

probs = la(data, pred_type=PredType.GLM, link_approx=LinkApprox.PROBIT)
print(probs.shape)

probs = la(data, pred_type=PredType.NN, link_approx=LinkApprox.MC, n_samples=10)
print(probs.shape)

torch.Size([4, 6, 20])
torch.Size([4, 6, 20])

The GLM predictive needs the Jacobian of all V logits at every token. For a real vocabulary, with tens of thousands of tokens, that does not fit in memory, so use the sampling predictive (pred_type="nn") there.

Caution

Every token is treated as an independent observation in the likelihood, i.e., the log-likelihood sums over all B * L tokens, not only over the B sequences. Padding tokens are not masked yet. They count toward the number of observations and, for most backends, toward the Hessian.

Last-layer Laplace (subset_of_weights="last_layer"), the BackPack backends, and FunctionalLaplace, ELLA, and VaLLA do not support outputs with more than 2 axes yet. For regression, the Kronecker-factored Hessian is only available with the Curvlinops backends; the ASDL backends raise an error.

docs.title: Sinusoidal toy data
docs.text:
We show how the marginal likelihood can be used after training a MAP network on a simple sinusoidal regression task. Subsequently, we use the optimized LA to predict which provides uncertainty on top of the MAP prediction. We also show how the marglik_training utility method can be used to jointly train the MAP and hyperparameters. First, we set up the training data for the problem with observation noise \(\sigma=0.3\):

from laplace.baselaplace import FullLaplace
from laplace.curvature.backpack import BackPackGGN
import numpy as np
import torch

from laplace import Laplace, marglik_training

from helper.dataloaders import get_sinusoid_example
from helper.util import plot_regression

n_epochs = 1000
torch.manual_seed(711)
# sample toy data example
X_train, y_train, train_loader, X_test = get_sinusoid_example(sigma_noise=0.3)

docs.title: Training a MAP
docs.text:
We now use pytorch to train a neural network with single hidden layer and Tanh activation. The trained neural network will be our MAP estimate. This is standard so nothing new here, yet:

# create and train MAP model
def get_model():
    torch.manual_seed(711)
    return torch.nn.Sequential(
        torch.nn.Linear(1, 50), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(50, 1)
    )
model = get_model()

criterion = torch.nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for i in range(n_epochs):
    for X, y in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(X), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

docs.title: Fitting and optimizing the Laplace approximation using empirical Bayes
docs.text:
With the MAP-trained model at hand, we can estimate the prior precision and observation noise using empirical Bayes after training. The Laplace method is called to construct a LA for "regression" with "all" weights. As default Laplace returns a Kronecker factored LA, we use "full" instead on this small example. We fit the LA to the training data and initialize log_prior and log_sigma. Using Adam, we minimize the negative log marginal likelihood for n_epochs.

la = Laplace(model, "regression", subset_of_weights="all", hessian_structure="full")
la.fit(train_loader)
log_prior, log_sigma = torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True), torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True)
hyper_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([log_prior, log_sigma], lr=1e-1)
for i in range(n_epochs):
    hyper_optimizer.zero_grad()
    neg_marglik = - la.log_marginal_likelihood(log_prior.exp(), log_sigma.exp())
    neg_marglik.backward()
    hyper_optimizer.step()

The obtained observation noise is close to the ground truth with a value of \(\sigma \approx 0.28\) without the need for any validation data. The resulting prior precision is \(\delta \approx 0.10\).

docs.title: Bayesian predictive
docs.text:
Here, we compare the MAP prediction to the obtained LA prediction. For LA, we have a closed-form predictive distribution on the output \(f\) which is a Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(f(x;\theta\_{MAP}), \mathbb{V}[f] + \sigma^2)\):

x = X_test.flatten().cpu().numpy()
f_mu, f_var = la(X_test)
f_mu = f_mu.squeeze().detach().cpu().numpy()
f_sigma = f_var.squeeze().sqrt().cpu().numpy()
pred_std = np.sqrt(f_sigma**2 + la.sigma_noise.item()**2)

plot_regression(X_train, y_train, x, f_mu, pred_std)

In comparison to the MAP, the predictive shows useful uncertainties. When our MAP is over or underfit, the Laplace approximation cannot fix this anymore. In this case, joint optimization of MAP and marginal likelihood can be useful.

docs.title: Jointly optimize MAP and hyperparameters using online empirical Bayes
docs.text:
We provide a utility method marglik_training that implements the algorithm proposed in [1]. The method optimizes the neural network and the hyperparameters in an interleaved way and returns an optimally regularized LA. Below, we use this method and plot the corresponding predictive uncertainties again:

model = get_model()
la, model, margliks, losses = marglik_training(
    model=model, train_loader=train_loader, likelihood="regression",
    hessian_structure="full", backend=BackPackGGN, n_epochs=n_epochs,
    optimizer_kwargs={"lr": 1e-2}, prior_structure="scalar"
)

f_mu, f_var = la(X_test)
f_mu = f_mu.squeeze().detach().cpu().numpy()
f_sigma = f_var.squeeze().sqrt().cpu().numpy()
pred_std = np.sqrt(f_sigma**2 + la.sigma_noise.item()**2)

plot_regression(X_train, y_train, x, f_mu, pred_std)

docs.title: Example: Reward Modeling
docs.text: The laplace-torch library can also be used to "Bayesianize" a pretrained Bradley-Terry reward model, popular in large language models. See http://arxiv.org/abs/2009.01325 for a primer in reward modeling.

docs.title: Defining a preference dataset
docs.text:
First order of business, let's define our comparison dataset. We will use the datasets library from Huggingface to handle the data.

import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn, optim
from torch.nn import functional as F
import torch.utils.data as data_utils

from datasets import Dataset

from laplace import Laplace

import logging
import warnings

logging.basicConfig(level="ERROR")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# make deterministic
torch.manual_seed(0)
np.random.seed(0)


# Pairwise comparison dataset. The label indicates which `x0` or `x1` is preferred.
data_dict = [
    {
        "x0": torch.randn(3),
        "x1": torch.randn(3),
        "label": torch.randint(2, size=(1,)).item(),
    }
    for _ in range(10)
]
dataset = Dataset.from_list(data_dict)

docs.title: Defining a reward model
docs.text:
Now, let's define the reward model. During training, it assumes that x is a tensor of shape (batch_size, 2, dim), which is a concatenation of x0 and x1 above. The second dimension of size 2 is preserved through the forward pass, resulting in a logit tensor of shape (batch_size, 2) (the network itself is single-output). Then, the standard cross-entropy loss is applied.

Note that this requirement is quite weak and can covers general cases. However, if you prefer to use the dict-like inputs as in Huggingface LLM models, this can also be done. Simply combine what you have learned from this example with the Huggingface LLM example provided in this library.

During testing, this model behaves like a standard single-output regression model.

class SimpleRewardModel(nn.Module):
    """A simple reward model, compatible with the Bradley-Terry likelihood.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 100), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(100, 1))

    def forward(self, x):
        """Args:
            x: torch.Tensor
                If training == True then shape (batch_size, 2, dim)
                Else shape (batch_size, dim)

        Returns:
            logits: torch.Tensor
                If training then shape (batch_size, 2)
                Else shape (batch_size, 1)
        """
        if len(x.shape) == 3:
            batch_size, _, dim = x.shape

            # Flatten to (batch_size*2, dim)
            flat_x = x.reshape(-1, dim)

            # Forward
            flat_logits = self.net(flat_x)  # (batch_size*2, 1)

            # Reshape back to (batch_size, 2)
            return flat_logits.reshape(batch_size, 2)
        else:
            logits = self.net(x)  # (batch_size, 1)
            return logits

docs.title: Data preprocessing
docs.text:
To fulfill the 3D tensor requirement, we need to preprocess the dict-based dataset.

# Preprocess to coalesce x0 and x1 into a single array/tensor
def append_x0_x1(row):
    # The tensor values above are automatically casted as lists by `Dataset`
    row["x"] = np.stack([row["x0"], row["x1"]])  # (2, dim)
    return row


tensor_dataset = dataset.map(append_x0_x1, remove_columns=["x0", "x1"])
tensor_dataset.set_format(type="torch", columns=["x", "label"])
columns = tensor_dataset[:]  # Dict of tensors; `tensor_dataset["x"]` may be lazy
tensor_dataloader = data_utils.DataLoader(
    data_utils.TensorDataset(columns["x"], columns["label"]), batch_size=3
)

docs.title: MAP training
docs.text:
Then, we can train as usual using the cross entropy loss.

reward_model = SimpleRewardModel()
opt = optim.AdamW(reward_model.parameters(), weight_decay=1e-3)

# Train as usual
for epoch in range(10):
    for x, y in tensor_dataloader:
        opt.zero_grad()
        out = reward_model(x)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(out, y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

docs.title: Applying Laplace
docs.text:
Applying Laplace to this model is a breeze. Simply state that the likelihood is reward_modeling.

# Laplace !!! Notice the likelihood !!!
reward_model.eval()
la = Laplace(reward_model, likelihood="reward_modeling", subset_of_weights="all")
la.fit(tensor_dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

As we can see, during prediction, even though we train & fit Laplace using the cross entropy loss (i.e. classification), in test time, the model behaves like a regression model. So, you don't get probability vectors as outputs. Instead, you get two tensors containing the predictive means and predictive variance.

x_test = torch.randn(5, 3)
pred_mean, pred_var = la(x_test)
print(
    f"Input shape {tuple(x_test.shape)}, predictive mean of shape "
    + f"{tuple(pred_mean.shape)}, predictive covariance of shape "
    + f"{tuple(pred_var.shape)}"
)

Here's the output:

Input shape (5, 3), predictive mean of shape (5, 1), predictive covariance of shape (5, 1, 1)

docs.title: Example: Semantic Segmentation
docs.text:
In this example, we apply Laplace to semantic segmentation, i.e., classification with one prediction per pixel. The predictive gives a distribution over the classes at every pixel, from which we get a per-pixel uncertainty map.

Laplace expects the class axis to be the last one, e.g., (N, K) for standard classifiers or (N, L, K) for language models. Convolutional models in PyTorch instead return logits (N, K, H, W), with the classes on axis 1. Laplace does not reorder the output for you, so you need to wrap your model so that it returns (N, H, W, K). The wrapper is a single movedim call. The targets are the usual class indices of shape (N, H, W) and do not need to change.

Intended usage

The wrapped model must return logits (N, H, W, K), and the targets must be class indices (N, H, W). Every pixel is an observation in the likelihood, i.e., the log-likelihood sums over all N * H * W pixels.

First, the imports and some constants.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

from laplace import Laplace
from laplace.curvature import CurvlinopsGGN

torch.manual_seed(0)

N_DATA = 64
CHANNELS = 3  # C
HEIGHT = 8  # H
WIDTH = 8  # W
N_CLASSES = 5  # K

Next, we define a toy segmentation network. It returns per-pixel logits in PyTorch's usual (N, K, H, W) layout. In practice, this would be your U-Net or similar.

class SegmentationNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.body = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(CHANNELS, 16, 3, padding=1),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(16, 16, 3, padding=1),
            nn.SiLU(),
        )
        self.head = nn.Conv2d(16, N_CLASSES, 1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.body(x))  # (N, K, H, W)

docs.title: Wrapping the model
docs.text:
The wrapper moves the class axis of the logits to the end.

class ClassesLast(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, net: nn.Module) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.net = net

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.net(x).movedim(1, -1)  # (N, H, W, K)

We use random images and masks in place of a real segmentation data set.

images = torch.randn(N_DATA, CHANNELS, HEIGHT, WIDTH)
masks = torch.randint(N_CLASSES, (N_DATA, HEIGHT, WIDTH))
dataloader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(images, masks), batch_size=16)
X, _ = next(iter(dataloader))

model = ClassesLast(SegmentationNet())
# Train it as usual
model.eval()

print(f"Output of the original model: {tuple(model.net(X).shape)}")
print(f"Output of the wrapped model: {tuple(model(X).shape)}")

Output of the original model: (16, 5, 8, 8)
Output of the wrapped model: (16, 8, 8, 5)

docs.title: Fitting Laplace
docs.text:
Segmentation networks are usually large, so we use a K-FAC Hessian over all weights. K-FAC with the Curvlinops backends supports nn.Linear and nn.Conv2d layers only. Segmentation networks often also have normalization layers, e.g., nn.BatchNorm2d or nn.GroupNorm, and nn.ConvTranspose2d for upsampling. If those have trainable parameters, fit raises a NotImplementedError. Either freeze them, so that the Laplace approximation only covers the other layers, or use hessian_structure="diag", which supports them. The toy network above has no such layers, so the following does nothing here.

for module in model.modules():
    if isinstance(module, (nn.BatchNorm2d, nn.GroupNorm, nn.ConvTranspose2d)):
        for p in module.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False

Note that we set subset_of_weights="all" explicitly. The default, "last_layer", requires an nn.Linear last layer, so it fails for a convolutional head.

la = Laplace(
    model,
    "classification",
    subset_of_weights="all",
    hessian_structure="kron",
    backend=CurvlinopsGGN,
)
la.fit(dataloader)
la.optimize_prior_precision()

docs.title: Predictive and uncertainty map
docs.text:
The GLM predictive returns the class probabilities of every pixel, in the wrapped layout (N, H, W, K). Their entropy is a per-pixel uncertainty map.

probs = la(X, pred_type="glm", link_approx="probit")
print(f"[GLM] Probabilities: {tuple(probs.shape)}")

entropy = -(probs * probs.log()).sum(dim=-1)
print(f"[GLM] Entropy: {tuple(entropy.shape)}")

[GLM] Probabilities: (16, 8, 8, 5)
[GLM] Entropy: (16, 8, 8)

To get back to PyTorch's layout, e.g., for plotting, undo the movedim:

probs = probs.movedim(-1, 1)
print(f"[GLM] Probabilities in (N, K, H, W): {tuple(probs.shape)}")

[GLM] Probabilities in (N, K, H, W): (16, 5, 8, 8)

The GLM predictive needs the Jacobian of the H * W * K logits of every image with respect to the weights in the Laplace approximation. For large images, that does not fit in memory. The sampling predictive runs the model once per weight sample from the posterior instead and never computes the Jacobian.

probs = la(X, pred_type="nn", link_approx="mc", n_samples=20)
print(f"[NN] Probabilities: {tuple(probs.shape)}")

[NN] Probabilities: (16, 8, 8, 5)

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Use the Curvlinops backends (CurvlinopsGGN, CurvlinopsEF). The ASDL and BackPACK backends raise an error for image outputs.
  • subset_of_weights="last_layer" requires an nn.Linear last layer. For a convolutional head, switch off the gradients of all other layers and use subset_of_weights="all", as in the diffusion example.
  • The targets must be class indices. Class probabilities as targets are not supported for image outputs.
  • Pixels labeled with -100 (PyTorch's default ignore_index), e.g., void pixels, are skipped by the loss, but still count toward the number of observations. With CurvlinopsGGN, they also still count toward the K-FAC Hessian used on this page and toward the diagonal Hessian. The full Hessian and the CurvlinopsEF backend leave them out. Masking them everywhere is tracked in #313.

The full script is in examples/segmentation_example.py.

docs.title: BaseLaplace
docs.text:
BaseLaplace(
    model: Module,
    likelihood: Likelihood | str,
    sigma_noise: float | Tensor = 1.0,
    prior_precision: float | Tensor = 1.0,
    prior_mean: float | Tensor = 0.0,
    temperature: float = 1.0,
    enable_backprop: bool = False,
    dict_key_x: str = "input_ids",
    dict_key_y: str = "labels",
    backend: type[CurvatureInterface] | None = None,
    backend_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    asdl_fisher_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
)

Baseclass for all Laplace approximations in this library.

Parameters:

  • model (Module) –
  • likelihood (Likelihood or str in {'classification', 'regression', 'reward_modeling'}) –

    determines the log likelihood Hessian approximation. In the case of 'reward_modeling', it fits Laplace using the classification likelihood, then does prediction as in regression likelihood. The model needs to be defined accordingly: The forward pass during training takes x.shape == (batch_size, 2, dim) with y.shape = (batch_size,). Meanwhile, during evaluation x.shape == (batch_size, dim). Reward modeling is supported by KronLaplace, DiagLaplace, ELLA, and VaLLA.

  • sigma_noise (Tensor or float, default: 1 ) –

    observation noise for the regression setting; must be 1 for classification

  • prior_precision (Tensor or float, default: 1 ) –

    prior precision of a Gaussian prior (= weight decay); can be scalar, per-layer, or diagonal in the most general case

  • prior_mean (Tensor or float, default: 0 ) –

    prior mean of a Gaussian prior, useful for continual learning

  • temperature (float, default: 1 ) –

    temperature of the likelihood; lower temperature leads to more concentrated posterior and vice versa.

  • enable_backprop (bool, default: False ) –

    whether to enable backprop to the input x through the Laplace predictive. Useful for e.g. Bayesian optimization.

  • dict_key_x (str, default: 'input_ids' ) –

    The dictionary key under which the input tensor x is stored. Only has effect when the model takes a MutableMapping as the input. Useful for Huggingface LLM models.

  • dict_key_y (str, default: 'labels' ) –

    The dictionary key under which the target tensor y is stored. Only has effect when the model takes a MutableMapping as the input. Useful for Huggingface LLM models.

  • backend (subclasses of `laplace.curvature.CurvatureInterface`, default: None ) –

    backend for access to curvature/Hessian approximations. Defaults to CurvlinopsGGN if None.

  • backend_kwargs (dict, default: None ) –

    arguments passed to the backend on initialization, for example to set the number of MC samples for stochastic approximations.

  • asdl_fisher_kwargs (dict, default: None ) –

    arguments passed to the ASDL backend specifically on initialization.

Source code in laplace/baselaplace.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    model: nn.Module,
    likelihood: Likelihood | str,
    sigma_noise: float | torch.Tensor = 1.0,
    prior_precision: float | torch.Tensor = 1.0,
    prior_mean: float | torch.Tensor = 0.0,
    temperature: float = 1.0,
    enable_backprop: bool = False,
    dict_key_x: str = "input_ids",
    dict_key_y: str = "labels",
    backend: type[CurvatureInterface] | None = None,
    backend_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    asdl_fisher_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None:
    if likelihood not in [lik.value for lik in Likelihood]:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid likelihood type {likelihood}")

    self.model: nn.Module = model
    self.likelihood: Likelihood | str = likelihood

    # Only do Laplace on params that require grad
    self.params: list[torch.Tensor] = []
    self.is_subset_params: bool = False
    for p in model.parameters():
        if p.requires_grad:
            self.params.append(p)
        else:
            self.is_subset_params = True

    self.n_params: int = sum(p.numel() for p in self.params)
    self.n_layers: int = len(self.params)
    self.prior_precision: float | torch.Tensor = prior_precision
    self.prior_mean: float | torch.Tensor = prior_mean
    if sigma_noise != 1 and likelihood != Likelihood.REGRESSION:
        raise ValueError("Sigma noise != 1 only available for regression.")

    self.sigma_noise: float | torch.Tensor = sigma_noise
    self.temperature: float = temperature
    self.enable_backprop: bool = enable_backprop

    # For models with dict-like inputs (e.g. Huggingface LLMs)
    self.dict_key_x = dict_key_x
    self.dict_key_y = dict_key_y

    if backend is None:
        backend = CurvlinopsGGN
    else:
        if self.is_subset_params and issubclass(
            backend, (BackPackInterface, AsdfghjklInterface)
        ):
            raise ValueError(
                "If some grad are switched off, the BackPACK and Asdfghjkl backends"
                " are not supported."
            )

    self._backend: CurvatureInterface | None = None
    self._backend_cls: type[CurvatureInterface] = backend
    self._backend_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = (
        dict() if backend_kwargs is None else backend_kwargs
    )
    self._asdl_fisher_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = (
        dict() if asdl_fisher_kwargs is None else asdl_fisher_kwargs
    )

    # log likelihood = g(loss)
    self.loss: float | torch.Tensor = 0.0
    self.n_outputs: int = 0
    self.n_data: int = 0
    # Number of observations in the likelihood. Differs from `n_data` only when
    # each datum has extra (e.g. sequence) dims: then it counts all tokens.
    self.n_obs: int = 0

    # Declare attributes
    self._prior_mean: torch.Tensor
    self._prior_precision: torch.Tensor
    self._sigma_noise: torch.Tensor
    self._posterior_scale: torch.Tensor | None

docs.title: __call__
docs.text:
__call__(
    x: Tensor | MutableMapping[str, Tensor | Any],
    pred_type: PredType | str = PredType.GLM,
    joint: bool = False,
    link_approx: LinkApprox | str = LinkApprox.PROBIT,
    n_samples: int = 100,
    diagonal_output: bool = False,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
    fitting: bool = False,
    **model_kwargs: dict[str, Any]
) -> Tensor | tuple[Tensor, Tensor]

Compute the posterior predictive on input data x.

Parameters:

  • x (Tensor or MutableMapping) –

    (batch_size, input_shape) if tensor. If MutableMapping, must contain the said tensor.

  • pred_type (('glm', 'nn'), default: 'glm' ) –

    type of posterior predictive, linearized GLM predictive or neural network sampling predictive. The GLM predictive is consistent with the curvature approximations used here. It also works when Laplace is done on a subset of the parameters, either with subnetwork Laplace or by disabling the gradients of the other parameters.

  • link_approx (('mc', 'probit', 'bridge', 'bridge_norm'), default: 'mc' ) –

    how to approximate the classification link function for the 'glm'. For pred_type='nn', only 'mc' is possible.

  • joint (bool, default: False ) –

    Whether to output a joint predictive distribution in regression with pred_type='glm'. If set to True, the predictive distribution has the same form as GP posterior, i.e. N([f(x1), ...,f(xm)], Cov[f(x1), ..., f(xm)]). If False, then only outputs the marginal predictive distribution. Only available for regression and GLM predictive.

  • n_samples (int, default: 100 ) –

    number of samples for link_approx='mc'.

  • diagonal_output (bool, default: False ) –

    whether to use a diagonalized posterior predictive on the outputs. Only works for pred_type='glm' when joint=False in regression. In the case of last-layer Laplace with a diagonal or Kron Hessian, setting this to True makes computation much(!) faster for large number of outputs.

  • generator (Generator, default: None ) –

    random number generator to control the samples (if sampling used).

  • fitting (bool, default: False ) –

    whether or not this predictive call is done during fitting. Only useful for reward modeling: the likelihood is set to "regression" when False and "classification" when True.

Returns:

  • predictive ( Tensor or tuple[Tensor] ) –

    For likelihood='classification', a torch.Tensor is returned with a distribution over classes (similar to a Softmax), with the same shape as the logits, e.g. (batch, classes) or (batch, seq_len, classes). For likelihood='regression', a tuple of torch.Tensor is returned with the mean and the predictive variance. For likelihood='regression' and joint=True, a tuple of torch.Tensor is returned with the mean and the predictive covariance.

def __call__(
    self,
    x: torch.Tensor | MutableMapping[str, torch.Tensor | Any],
    pred_type: PredType | str = PredType.GLM,
    joint: bool = False,
    link_approx: LinkApprox | str = LinkApprox.PROBIT,
    n_samples: int = 100,
    diagonal_output: bool = False,
    generator: torch.Generator | None = None,
    fitting: bool = False,
    **model_kwargs: dict[str, Any],
) -> torch.Tensor | tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """Compute the posterior predictive on input data `x`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x : torch.Tensor or MutableMapping
        `(batch_size, input_shape)` if tensor. If MutableMapping, must contain
        the said tensor.

    pred_type : {'glm', 'nn'}, default='glm'
        type of posterior predictive, linearized GLM predictive or neural
        network sampling predictive. The GLM predictive is consistent with
        the curvature approximations used here. It also works when Laplace
        is done on a subset of the parameters, either with subnetwork
        Laplace or by disabling the gradients of the other parameters.

    link_approx : {'mc', 'probit', 'bridge', 'bridge_norm'}
        how to approximate the classification link function for the `'glm'`.
        For `pred_type='nn'`, only 'mc' is possible.

    joint : bool
        Whether to output a joint predictive distribution in regression with
        `pred_type='glm'`. If set to `True`, the predictive distribution
        has the same form as GP posterior, i.e. N([f(x1), ...,f(xm)], Cov[f(x1), ..., f(xm)]).
        If `False`, then only outputs the marginal predictive distribution.
        Only available for regression and GLM predictive.

    n_samples : int, default=100
        number of samples for `link_approx='mc'`.

    diagonal_output : bool
        whether to use a diagonalized posterior predictive on the outputs.
        Only works for `pred_type='glm'` when `joint=False` in regression.
        In the case of last-layer Laplace with a diagonal or Kron Hessian,
        setting this to `True` makes computation much(!) faster for large
        number of outputs.

    generator : torch.Generator, optional
        random number generator to control the samples (if sampling used).

    fitting : bool, default=False
        whether or not this predictive call is done during fitting. Only useful for
        reward modeling: the likelihood is set to `"regression"` when `False` and
        `"classification"` when `True`.

    Returns
    -------
    predictive: torch.Tensor or tuple[torch.Tensor]
        For `likelihood='classification'`, a torch.Tensor is returned with
        a distribution over classes (similar to a Softmax), with the same shape
        as the logits, e.g. `(batch, classes)` or `(batch, seq_len, classes)`.
        For `likelihood='regression'`, a tuple of torch.Tensor is returned
        with the mean and the predictive variance.
        For `likelihood='regression'` and `joint=True`, a tuple of torch.Tensor
        is returned with the mean and the predictive covariance.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError

docs.text:
optimize_prior_precision(
    pred_type: PredType | str,
    method: TuningMethod | str = TuningMethod.MARGLIK,
    n_steps: int = 100,
    lr: float = 0.1,
    init_prior_prec: float | Tensor = 1.0,
    prior_structure: (
        PriorStructure | str
    ) = PriorStructure.DIAG,
    val_loader: DataLoader | None = None,
    loss: (
        Metric | Callable[[Tensor], Tensor | float] | None
    ) = None,
    log_prior_prec_min: float = -4,
    log_prior_prec_max: float = 4,
    grid_size: int = 100,
    link_approx: LinkApprox | str = LinkApprox.PROBIT,
    n_samples: int = 100,
    verbose: bool = False,
    progress_bar: bool = False,
    log_prior_prec_base: float = 10.0,
) -> None

Optimize the prior precision post-hoc using the method specified by the user.

Parameters:

  • pred_type (PredType or str in {'glm', 'nn'}) –

    type of posterior predictive, linearized GLM predictive or neural network sampling predictiv. The GLM predictive is consistent with the curvature approximations used here.

  • method (TuningMethod or str in {'marglik', 'gridsearch'}, default: PredType.MARGLIK ) –

    specifies how the prior precision should be optimized.

  • n_steps (int, default: 100 ) –

    the number of gradient descent steps to take.

  • lr (float, default: 1e-1 ) –

    the learning rate to use for gradient descent.

  • init_prior_prec (float or tensor, default: 1.0 ) –

    initial prior precision before the first optimization step.

  • prior_structure (PriorStructure or str in {'scalar', 'layerwise', 'diag'}, default: PriorStructure.SCALAR ) –

    if init_prior_prec is scalar, the prior precision is optimized with this structure. otherwise, the structure of init_prior_prec is maintained.

  • val_loader (DataLoader, default: None ) –

    DataLoader for the validation set; each iterate is a training batch (X, y).

  • loss (callable or Metric, default: None ) –

    loss function to use for CV. If callable, the loss is computed offline (memory intensive). If torchmetrics.Metric, running loss is computed (efficient). The default depends on the likelihood: RunningNLLMetric() for classification and reward modeling, running MeanSquaredError() for regression.

  • log_prior_prec_min (float, default: -4 ) –

    exponent of the lower bound of the gridsearch interval.

  • log_prior_prec_max (float, default: 4 ) –

    exponent of the upper bound of the gridsearch interval.

  • grid_size (int, default: 100 ) –

    number of values to consider inside the gridsearch interval.

  • link_approx (LinkApprox or str in {'mc', 'probit', 'bridge'}, default: LinkApprox.PROBIT ) –

    how to approximate the classification link function for the 'glm'. For pred_type='nn', only 'mc' is possible.

  • n_samples (int, default: 100 ) –

    number of samples for link_approx='mc'.

  • verbose (bool, default: False ) –

    if true, the optimized prior precision will be printed (can be a large tensor if the prior has a diagonal covariance).

  • progress_bar (bool, default: False ) –

    whether to show a progress bar; updated at every batch-Hessian computation. Useful for very large model and large amount of data, esp. when subset_of_weights='all'.

  • log_prior_prec_base (float, default: 10.0 ) –

    base of the logarithmic gridsearch interval. The bounds are log_prior_prec_base raised to log_prior_prec_min and log_prior_prec_max.
